title: Parker Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Parker wells have a 320-foot median depth; see yields, water levels, drilling costs, risks, and permit history near Parker.
h1: What Parker Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
Buying land near Parker means evaluating the well as part of the property, not as an afterthought. Permit records within five miles show a wide range of depths, but the typical well is completed in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and produces a useful household supply.

The records also show why a neighboring-well check matters. Some wells are in fractured bedrock, where depth and production can vary from lot to lot. Use these figures to question a seller, estimate a drilling budget, and decide what testing and site investigation should happen before closing.

sections.heading: Parker well depths run deeper than many buyers expect
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Parker is 320 feet deep. The middle half runs from 210 to 485 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the conditions at a particular lot. The 90th percentile is 646 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 2,745 feet.

Depth records are concentrated in the middle range: 41% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Fifteen percent are under 100 feet, and another 15% exceed 600 feet. The aquifers named most often are the Lower Dawson, Upper Dawson, and unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer.

For a driller's proposal, ask what depth assumption is included, when extra footage is billed, and how casing and grout will be handled.

sections.heading: Most Parker wells make enough for a home, but verify the test
sections.html:
Among nearby records that report a pump yield, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-six percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 44% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset. That is encouraging for a normal household, but it is not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. A yield test is a snapshot, and storage capacity, pump sizing, household demand, and permit conditions still matter.

Ask for the well construction report, pump test, and current production information. A domestic or household-use permit may have limits, and an exempt household-use well is not the same as an unlimited irrigation source.

sections.heading: Parker water levels vary, so the decade record needs context
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 195 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 100 to 395 feet. That range affects pump setting, electrical planning, and the cost of getting water from the wellhead to the house.

The decade medians do not form a steady downward pattern. Reported depth to water was 114 feet in the 1970s, 230 feet in the 1980s, 441 feet in the 2000s, 285 feet in the 2010s, and 160 feet in the 2020s. Different wells, locations, aquifers, and measurement conditions can drive that variation.

Do not treat the series as proof that Parker's water table is simply dropping or recovering. Get the static level for the subject well and have the pump contractor size equipment around actual conditions.

sections.heading: Parker's permit history shows long local drilling experience
sections.html:
DWR records include 4,842 permitted wells within five miles of Parker, with 2,613 recorded as constructed. The permits span several decades, and the newest permit year is 2025. The largest permit totals are from the 1970s and 1980s, with 877 and 947 permits respectively.

The most active drillers in these records are Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J), and Parker Drilling/Pump Service Inc. (Thrasher, Tommy E.). Those names identify local permit history, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability.

Before hiring anyone, confirm licensing, insurance, schedule, casing and grout specifications, pump-test terms, and who handles the DWR paperwork. A driller should also explain how the estimate changes if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: A median-depth Parker well can cost $22,000 to $34,400 finished
sections.html:
In Parker's Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 320-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $16,000 to $22,400.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at about $22,000 to $34,400 at that median depth. This is a planning range, not a fixed bid. A well near the deep end of the local range can add substantial drilling cost before the pump and site work are included.

Request a written proposal that separates footage, casing, grout, well development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, permits, and water testing. Also ask what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than the target yield. Those terms matter as much as the per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low-yield risk, and the building site
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 77 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 7 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not establish contamination in a particular well, but they are a reason to review site history, well location, groundwater flow, and laboratory testing before relying on the water.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks, especially where fractured bedrock controls production. Test the existing well for bacteria, nitrate, and locally relevant contaminants, and ask a qualified professional whether PFAS or other testing is appropriate.

Confirm septic setbacks, reserve area, driveway access, electrical routing, and the buildable envelope before closing. Water rights also matter: augmentation plans may be required in over-appropriated basins, and the permit's allowed use controls what the well can legally serve.

sections.heading: Use neighboring wells to plan a Parker lot
sections.html:
For an existing home, start with the actual well permit, construction report, pump information, production history, and a recent water-quality test. Compare those records with nearby wells in Stonegate, Stepping Stone, Sierra Ridge, Meridian Village, Grand View Estates, and The Pinery when the locations are relevant to the property. Neighboring records can reveal likely depth and aquifer conditions, but they cannot replace a site-specific inspection.

For vacant land, make the well plan part of due diligence. Confirm the permit pathway with Colorado DWR, identify the legal use, reserve room for the well and septic system, and price access for a drilling rig. Carry a budget that recognizes the local depth spread rather than assuming every hole will match the median.

Before you build, have the driller, septic designer, electrician, and excavator coordinate the wellhead, tank, trench, driveway, and house location.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Parker, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Parker is 320 feet. The middle half runs from 210 to 485 feet, while 41% are between 300 and 600 feet. Some wells exceed 600 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 2,745 feet. The exact depth depends on the lot, aquifer, and fractured-bedrock conditions.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Parker?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 320-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $16,000 to $22,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $22,000 to $34,400. A written bid should explain extra footage and included equipment.

faq.q: How much water do Parker wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 14.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-six percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 44% report more than 15. These figures describe permitted records, not a guarantee for a new well or a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Parker?
faq.a: A well's safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Nearby mapped records include 77 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 7 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property well through a qualified laboratory and review local site history before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are Parker well water levels dropping?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a simple continuous decline. Depth to water was 114 feet in the 1970s, 441 feet in the 2000s, and 160 feet in the 2020s, with other decades between those values. The changes may reflect different wells and measurement conditions, so obtain the static level for the specific property.
